questions.question: How do you answer behavioral interview questions?
questions.title: Answering Behavioral Questions
questions.direct_answer: Behavioral questions ('Tell me about a time you faced a conflict', 'Describe a hard bug') test how you act, not what you know. You answer with the STAR method: Situation (the context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what YOU did), Result (the outcome, ideally with numbers). The interviewer wants a specific real story, not a general opinion — so pick a concrete example, keep the situation brief, spend most of the time on YOUR action, and end with the measurable result and what you learned. Prepare 3-5 flexible stories (a bug, a conflict, a deadline, a learning) you can adapt to many questions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you use STAR (Situation/Task/Action/Result) with a specific story and spend most of the time on your action and the result.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a vague opinion instead of a specific story, or talking about the team's action instead of YOUR action.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use STAR: Situation (context), Task (your role), Action (what YOU did), Result (outcome + numbers). Spend most of the time on YOUR action and the result.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define Answering Behavioral Questions simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: The STAR Method
sections.content: Behavioral questions — 'Tell me about a time you faced a conflict', 'Describe a hard bug' — test how you act, not what you know. You answer with the STAR method: Situation (the context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what YOU did), Result (the outcome, ideally with numbers). The interviewer wants a specific real story, not a general opinion, so pick a concrete example, keep the situation brief, spend most of the time on YOUR action, and end with the measurable result and what you learned. Prepare 3-5 flexible stories — a bug, a conflict, a deadline, a learning — you can adapt to many questions, so you're never stuck inventing a story on the spot.

sections.title: STAR Flow
sections.content:
Situation -> Task -> Action (most of the time) -> Result.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[Situation: context] --> T[Task: your role]
  T --> A[Action: what YOU did]
  A --> R[Result: outcome + numbers]
```

sections.title: A STAR answer (abbreviated)
sections.content:
```ruby
# Q: 'Tell me about a time you fixed a hard bug.'
# STAR answer:

# S: 'Our Rails app's nightly job was timing out for 2k users.'
# T: 'I owned the job; I had one day before it affected customers.'
# A: 'I read the logs, found an N+1 query (a .each loading comments per user),
#     added Post.includes(:comments), and added an index on post_id.
#     I tested locally with a 2k-row fixture, then deployed.'
# R: 'The job went from 40 min to 90 sec (~26x), and no more timeouts.'
# (Most of the time is on A; R has a number.)
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Giving a vague opinion ('I think conflict is...') instead of a specific story.
Talking about the team's action instead of YOUR action — the interviewer wants what you did.
No measurable result — add a number (time saved, bugs down, users affected).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Behavioral questions test how you act; answer with STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result).
Pick a SPECIFIC real story, not a general opinion; keep the situation brief.
Spend most of the time on YOUR action and the measurable result.
End with a number (time saved, % improvement) and what you learned.
Prepare 3-5 flexible stories (bug, conflict, deadline, learning) you can adapt.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Behavioral questions — 'Tell me about a time you faced a conflict', 'Describe a hard bug' — test how you act, not what you know. You answer with the STAR method: Situation, the context; Task, your responsibility; Action, what you did; Result, the outcome, ideally with numbers. The interviewer wants a specific real story, not a general opinion, so pick a concrete example, keep the situation brief, spend most of the time on your action, and end with the measurable result and what you learned. A common mistake is giving a vague opinion instead of a specific story, or talking about the team's action instead of your action, when the interviewer wants what you did, and no measurable result, when you should add a number like time saved or bugs down. Prepare three to five flexible stories — a bug, a conflict, a deadline, a learning — you can adapt to many questions.

sections.title: Concept explained
sections.content: Walk through the example step by step, then say when this approach is a good fit and what you would test at the boundary.
